Cardiology and hematology · published research

Carotid artery stenosis

The newer of two related mouse studies reported higher regional cerebral perfusion, improved cognitive-test performance, and less neuronal loss after experimentally induced carotid narrowing, although necrotic foci remained. Neither study tested people, plaque removal, or stroke prevention.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

The newer of two related mouse studies reported higher regional cerebral perfusion, improved cognitive-test performance, and less neuronal loss after experimentally induced carotid narrowing, although necrotic foci remained. Neither study tested people, plaque removal, or stroke prevention.

Summary of the Evidence

Two original publications were identified through the carotid-stenosis category. Both used mice with surgically induced bilateral common-carotid narrowing or chronic cerebral hypoperfusion. They are separate reports, but both come from a closely related Korean research setting and use a similar model family, so they do not provide broad independent replication. No human treatment study or carotid-stenosis-specific cell experiment was identified. A related 2019 conference proceeding by the same research group appears to describe the near-infrared mouse project and is not counted as a separate independent experiment (Lee et al. 2019 Kim et al. 2026).

Human and clinical evidence

No clinical study has tested PBM in people with carotid artery stenosis. The experiments concern the effects of light on brain tissue after experimentally reduced blood flow; they do not test whether light removes plaque, widens the artery, prevents stroke, or replaces established vascular care.

Animal evidence

The 2019 study used three groups of mice, with approximately four to five animals per group. After bilateral common-carotid stenosis, near-infrared LED treatment was directed at the top of the head. Positron-emission tomography was used to measure whole-brain and regional cerebral blood flow. The report describes the system and perfusion assessment but remains a small conference-proceedings study (Lee et al. 2019, Optica/SPIE proceedings, Source).

The 2026 journal report used a mouse model of chronic cerebral hypoperfusion and found higher regional blood flow, particularly in cortical and hippocampal areas, alongside improved cognitive-test performance. Histology showed less neuronal loss and smaller perivascular spaces, although necrotic foci remained. Changes in BCL2 and HIF-1 were also reported. These outcomes suggest a biological response in the model, but not reversal of human carotid disease (Kim et al. 2026).

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No separate cell-culture or ex-vivo study specific to carotid stenosis was identified. Tissue-marker measurements from the mouse experiment are part of the animal study and should not be counted as an independent laboratory publication.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The 2019 protocol used an 810 nm near-infrared LED, which is invisible light beyond the visible red band, at 20 mW directed transcranially from above the mouse head, three times per week for one month. The accessible abstract for the 2026 paper does not provide enough dosimetry detail to compare its dose with the earlier protocol. No head-to-head wavelength or dose-finding study was identified. Light transmission through a mouse head does not by itself establish what dose reaches a human brain through a larger scalp and skull.

Interpretation

In the newer mouse study, regional cerebral perfusion and cognitive-test performance improved, while neuronal loss and perivascular changes were reduced; necrotic foci remained. A related earlier report also examined light exposure in a carotid-narrowing model. These are favorable brain-model outcomes, not evidence that PBM widens human carotids, removes plaque, or prevents stroke.

Evidence strength in source summaryVery low for cerebral blood-flow or cognitive outcomes in carotid stenosis
Publications and records2 articles

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

Two related mouse publications examine brain effects of experimentally induced carotid narrowing. The newer reported higher regional perfusion, better cognitive-test performance, and less neuronal loss, although necrotic foci remained. These are favorable model-level findings, not evidence that light removes carotid plaque or prevents stroke. Independent replication and well-reported delivery parameters would clarify clinical relevance.
